full_judgment:
58. Now turning to Exhibit XI, a letter said to have written by Mr Joydeb Mojumder to the Police Commissioner which is used as another circumstantial evidence. In course of cross-examination, PW 48 admitted that in the letter Titu's name was not mentioned. PW 32 also admitted that Titu's name was not mentioned in that letter. She, however, gave an explanation that “ ঐ চিঠিতে জয়দেব বাবু টিটুর নামটা এই কারনে লিখেন নাই যে টিটু বিখ্যাত শিল্পপতির ছেলে বিধায় তাহার নাম লিখিলে ভবিষ্যতে ঝামেলা হইতে পারে। This explanation can only be given by Mr Joydeb and not by PW 32. What prompted Mr Joydeb in not mentioning Titu's name could only be explained by him. She being not the author of the letter is not legally entitled to give explanation on behalf of the author of the letter. Besides, this is a lame excuse because if Jibran was apprehensive of his life and sought help from the then Assistant High Commissioner for bringing the matter to the higher police authority, the natural presumption is that he had furnished the name of the person who had threatened him to death and there was no reason on the part of Mr Joydeb not to mention the name of Titu when he had written letter to a Police Commissioner for taking security measures for Jibran. During the relevant time there was none other than Titu who allegedly threatened him as disclosed in the evidence. So apparently the explanation furnished by PW 32 cannot be accepted. Further, this letter does not reveal that there is prima-facie evidence affording reasonable ground to believe that the appellant and other convicts have conspired to kill Jibran 

 93. Learned Additional Attorney-General, on the other hand, has referred the cases of Mobarak Hossain vs State, 33 DLR 274 and Al-Amin vs State, 51 DLR 75. In Mobarak Hossain, the High Court Division itself observed, It is true that mere fact of absconding is of little importance if there is nothing beyond that. Importance of the fact of absconding of accused will depend on the facts of each particular case.' In Al-Amin, the High Court Division observed 'Abscondence of the accused-persons furnished corroboration of the prosecution case and evidence'. In that case all convicted persons assaulted PWs 1, 2, 3 and then raped the victims, got the incident recorded by hiring a cameraman, and then they absconded. Therefore, this case is distinguishable from other cases on the principles discussed in Amir Hossain. In Abdul Khaleque (Supra), it was observed by the High Court Division that 'It is true mere absconsion of the accused after the occurrence is not sufficient to hold him guilty of the offence. But since the victim died in the house of the accused as a result of injuries who was none but the wife of the accused, the High Court Division rightly drew adverse presumption against the accused as he fled away from the house immediate after the occurrence. 

 97. The High Court Division observed, 'the defense could not bring on record either by cross-examining the prosecution witnesses by bringing any other material in other manner showing any involvement of Jibran or his connection with any person having any bad reputation or connection with any illegal business or trading including smuggling so that he might have developed any sort of animosity with others who might have been behind the killing’. The High Court Division lost sight of the fact that the defence need not prove how and why Jibran was assassinated? There might be thousand and one causes for the death and the defence is under no obligation to explain the cause of death. This is against the established principle of criminal jurisprudence prevailing in the administration of justice. I fail to understand why the High Court Division has made this observation and drawn adverse presumption against the defence only because Jibran was said to have been a man of good character. This finding is also inconsistent with its earlier findings. The High Court Division noticed that Jibran and Samanja were having secret love affair. This relationship with a young unmarried girl despite the fact that Jibran had an educated cultured wife proved that Jibran did not lead a decent life. If the evidence of PWs 6 and 32 are taken to be true, he was a man of ignominious character. 

 98. A presumption is a rule of law that courts shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact or from particular evidence unless the truth of such inference is disproved. One of the cardinal principles of our criminal jurisprudence is that an accused is presumed to be innocent unless his guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt. An accused-person is under no obligation to offer evidence and he is merely on the defensive and owes no duty to anyone but himself. He is at liberty, as to the whole case to rely on the witnesses of the case for the prosecution, and no inference unfavourable to him can properly be drawn because he takes one course rather than the other. 

 "The fundamental of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduce evidence to prove his innocence, but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence, whether the case is before the trial court or at higher forums In a criminal trial determination of a disputed fact is the main task before the court and such determination is dependent upon consideration of answers given by the prosecution in their cross-examination. Cross-examination is therefore indispensably necessary to bring out desirable facts of a case modifying the examination-in-chief or establishing the cross-examiner's own case. The object of cross-examination is twofold, to bring out desirable facts of a case modifying the examination-in-chief on establishing the cross-examiner's own case. 

 "We may say here that it is now the settled law that the powers of the High Court in an appeal against the acquittal are not different from the powers of the same Court in hearing an appeal against a conviction. The High Court in dealing with such an appeal can go into all questions of fact and law and reach its own conclusions on evidence provided 11 days due regard to the fact that the matter had been before the Court of Session and the Sessions Judge had the chance and opportunity of seeing the witnesses depose to the facts. Further the High Court in reversing the judgment of the Sessions Judge must pay due regard to all the reasons given by the Sessions Judge for disbelieving a particular witness and must attempt to dispel those reasons effectively before taking a contrary view of the matter. It may also be pointed out that an accused starts with a presumption of innocence when he is put up for trial and his acquittal in no sense weakens that presumption, and this presumption must also receive adequate consideration from the High Court". 

 112. The presumption of innocence is strengthened whenever an accused is acquitted. So, the High Court Division should keep in mind when it deals with an appeal against acquittal, the benefit of doubt be given in favour of the accused, not in favour of the prosecution and it will be slow in disturbing a finding of fact arrived at by the trial court particularly when the finding is based on proper appreciation of the evidence. This is because the trial Court has the advantage of evaluating the demeanour of the witnesses. It has been observed in MG Agarwal vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1963 SC 200, that "though the powers of the High Court in dealing with an appeal against acquittal are as wide as those which it has in dealing with an appeal against conviction, in dealing with former class of appeals, its approach is governed by the overriding consideration frowning from the presumption of innocence. Sometimes the width of the power is emphasized, while on the other occasions, the necessity to adopt a cautions approach in dealing with appeals against acquittals is emphasized, and the emphasis is expressed in different words or phrases used from time to time". 

 113. The above views have been taken with approval of the opinions expressed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup vs Emperor, AIR 1934 PC 227 and Nur Mohammad vi Emperor, AIR 1945 PC 151. The principle that only reasonable doubts belong to the accused has been accepted by superior courts with a few exceptions where administration of justice is different. Otherwise any practical systems of justice will then break down and lose credibility with the community. The onus to prove the different ingredients of the offence is on the prosecution and unless it discharges that onus, the prosecution cannot succeed. I have noticed on perusal of the impugned judgment, the High Court Division has ignored this established principle in this particular case and given the benefit and presumption in favour of the prosecution.
